clinicalPearls: Biallelic GJB2 (connexin 26) variants at the DFNB1 locus are the commonest single cause of hereditary sensorineural hearing loss in many populations
Hearing loss is typically congenital, bilateral, symmetrical, and non-progressive, ranging from mild to profound with no associated systemic features
The 35delG frameshift variant predominates in European-derived populations, while other founder variants (such as 235delC) are common elsewhere
A common cause of missed genotyping is a large GJB6 deletion in trans with a single GJB2 variant, so testing must consider the wider DFNB1 region
Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive with unaffected carrier parents, though rare dominant GJB2 variants exist and may co-segregate with skin phenotypes
Vestibular function is generally preserved, and imaging is usually normal, distinguishing it from malformation-related or syndromic causes
Cochlear implantation outcomes are typically excellent because the lesion is cochlear with an intact auditory nerve and central pathway
reference.pathophysiology: Connexin 26, encoded by GJB2, is a gap-junction protein expressed in the supporting cells and fibrocytes of the cochlea. Connexins assemble into intercellular channels that permit potassium and small-molecule movement, supporting recycling of potassium away from hair cells back to the endolymph and maintaining the endocochlear potential. Loss-of-function variants disrupt this gap-junction network, impairing potassium homeostasis and cochlear amplification, which produces sensorineural hearing loss without structural malformation. Because the deficit lies within the cochlear support apparatus rather than the auditory nerve, the phenotype is a pure cochlear sensorineural loss.
additionalDifferentials: Enlarged vestibular aqueduct and other inner-ear malformations
Acquired perinatal ototoxic or hypoxic injury
additionalInvestigations: Newborn hearing screening followed by diagnostic audiometry (age-appropriate behavioural or objective testing)
Otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response to characterise the site and severity of loss
Targeted GJB2 sequencing and assessment for GJB6 deletions across the DFNB1 locus
Comprehensive deafness gene panel when DFNB1 testing is uninformative
Cross-sectional temporal bone imaging to exclude structural anomalies before implantation
Congenital cytomegalovirus testing where the loss may be acquired
redFlags: Progressive or fluctuating loss, which is atypical and should prompt review for another cause such as EVA
Asymmetry or unilateral loss suggesting a structural or acquired lesion
Any associated dysmorphism, pigmentary, thyroid, renal, or visual features indicating a syndrome
Delayed speech and language development from unrecognised or under-amplified hearing loss
reference.prognosis: The hearing loss is usually stable over time, and because the auditory nerve and central pathways are intact, most children achieve good outcomes with early amplification or cochlear implantation and structured habilitation.
pitfalls: Assuming a single heterozygous GJB2 variant explains the phenotype without excluding a GJB6 deletion in trans
Overlooking congenital cytomegalovirus as a mimicking or coexisting cause
Delaying intervention while awaiting genetic results and missing the critical window for language acquisition
Attributing later progression solely to DFNB1 rather than reassessing for another disorder
references: GeneReviews: Nonsyndromic Hearing Loss and Deafness, DFNB1
management: Fit hearing aids early after diagnosis to provide auditory access during the critical period of language development
Refer for cochlear implantation when loss is severe to profound, since the intact auditory nerve predicts good outcomes
Provide structured habilitation with speech and language therapy and family-centred communication support
Undertake audiological surveillance to confirm the usually stable loss and adjust amplification as the child grows
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition, testing relatives and considering GJB6 deletions across the DFNB1 locus
Exclude structural anomalies with temporal bone imaging before implantation and confirm the loss is genetic rather than acquired
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary audiovestibular, otology, speech therapy and educational team
